title: The Impact of Psychological, Economic, Social Aspects, and Interest Rate Variations on Working Millennials' Saving Patterns Through Digital Banking
authors: Ataza, C.M.; Porcel, M.A.B.; Resabal, L.F.; Sandoval, A.E.G.; Bragas, C.M.
tldr: A survey of 51 working millennials in Metro Manila found that interest rate variations and psychological aspects significantly predict saving patterns through digital banking, while social aspects have a negative effect.
problem_and_motivation: Working millennials in the Philippines face complex financial decisions as digital banking proliferates, yet the combined influence of psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factors on their saving patterns through digital platforms remains underexplored. Understanding these factors is critical for digital banks seeking to optimize personalized offers and for policymakers promoting financial inclusion. Existing literature addresses individual factors in isolation but lacks an integrated analysis of their collective impact on saving behavior in the Philippine digital banking context.
approach: Surveyed 51 working millennials aged 26-42 who have bank accounts in Metro Manila, Philippines using purposive sampling.
Used a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire with 20 items across four constructs: psychological aspects, economic aspects, social aspects, and interest rate variations.
Applied Cronbach's alpha to assess internal consistency, with all constructs exceeding 0.8 (ranging from 0.804 to 0.926).
Conducted multiple linear regression analysis to determine the relative influence of each factor on saving patterns through digital banking.
Grounded the study in the Classical Theory of Interest and Theory of Planned Behavior as theoretical frameworks.
findings: Interest rate variations had the strongest positive effect on saving patterns (Beta = 0.878, p < 0.001), explaining approximately 70% of variance.
Psychological aspects had a significant positive effect (Beta = 0.430, p = 0.006), explaining 31.02% of variance in saving behaviors.
num: Social aspects had a significant negative effect (Beta = -0.182, p = 0.016), explaining only 8.47% of variance.
Economic aspects had a non-significant negative effect (Beta = -0.130, p = 0.293), explaining 26.42% of variance.
num: The combined model explained approximately 75.34% of variance in saving patterns through digital banking (R² = 0.7534).
num: 84.3% of respondents were aged 26-31, and 58.8% used both digital and traditional banks.
num: 58.8% of respondents were female, suggesting females save more through digital banking than males.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study contributes to the understanding of financial behavior among Filipino working millennials by integrating psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factors into a single regression model for digital banking saving patterns. It provides empirical evidence from the Philippine context that interest rate variations are the dominant predictor of saving behavior, explaining 70% of variance, while psychological factors contribute an additional 31%. The study identifies that social aspects have a counterintuitive negative effect, suggesting millennials prioritize personal financial goals over social pressures. These findings offer actionable insights for digital bank managers seeking to optimize saving products for the Philippine millennial market.

limits: Small sample size of 51 respondents limits statistical power and generalizability.
Purposive sampling may introduce selection bias.
Cross-sectional design does not capture temporal changes in saving behavior.
Single geographic focus on Metro Manila excludes rural and provincial millennials.
Self-reported Likert scale data may be subject to social desirability bias.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All topic domains were systematically scanned. The paper directly addresses Filipino young professionals (1.A, 1.B, 1.C) with high relevance, as the entire study focuses on working millennials in Metro Manila. User-declared financial preferences (2.C) receive high relevance through the survey-based methodology measuring psychological, economic, social, and interest rate factor preferences. The digital banking landscape (4.A) receives medium relevance as contextual background. Engagement dynamics (11.A, 11.B) receive medium and low relevance respectively, as the study examines factors driving saving engagement but does not focus on retention design. Topics on culturally specific practices (2.A, 2.B, 2.D), expense categorization (3.A-C), existing system limitations (4.B), financial behavioral profiles (5.A-C), predictive modeling (6.A-B), budgeting (7.A-E), anomaly detection (8.A-C), mobile design (9.A-C), privacy (10.A-C), savings/debt (13.A-C), and synthetic data (14.A-C) were considered and rejected as not directly covered.

limitations: Small sample size of 51 respondents limits statistical power and generalizability to the broader millennial population.
Purposive sampling technique may introduce selection bias among respondents.
Cross-sectional design does not capture temporal changes in saving behavior over time.
Single geographic focus on Metro Manila excludes rural and provincial millennials.
Self-reported Likert scale data may be subject to social desirability and response biases.
The study does not account for specific digital bank platform differences or features.
